request.contents:
Is this clause enforceable in a residential lease in Ontario? Cite the section.

Read the clause as a term of an ordinary private residential tenancy in Ontario that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 covers: the rental unit has no exemption under section 6.1, and it is not student housing, a care home, a co-operative or a mobile home park.

Clause: The Landlord may increase the rent by up to the guideline amount once in any 12-month period, after giving the Tenant at least 90 days' written notice in the form approved by the Landlord and Tenant Board.

End your answer with these two lines:
Verdict: enforceable (or: Verdict: not enforceable)
Section: <the number of the one section of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 that decides it>

text:
No, this clause is **not enforceable** in an Ontario residential lease.

While the clause complies with the notice requirements of section 116 (at least 90 days' written notice in the LTB-approved form) and the rent cap in section 120 (up to the guideline amount), its timing rule—**"once in any 12-month period"**—conflicts with **section 119** of the *Residential Tenancies Act, 2006* (and is therefore void under section 4).

Under **section 119(1)**, a landlord may increase the rent only if **at least 12 months have elapsed**:
* **(a)** since the day of the last rent increase for that tenant in that rental unit, if there has been a previous increase; or
* **(b)** **since the day the rental unit was first rented to that tenant**, in any other case.

Setting the initial lawful rent at the start of a tenancy (section 113) is not a "rent increase." Consequently, allowing an increase "once in any 12-month period" would permit the landlord to give 90 days' notice at the start of the tenancy and impose the first rent increase during the first 12 months of the tenancy (for example, in month 4), as long as the landlord then waited 12 months before increasing it again. Because that violates the mandatory 12-month waiting period from the start of the tenancy under section 119(1)(b), the clause is inconsistent with the Act and unenforceable.

Verdict: not enforceable
Section: 119
